story:
Kayla read her story aloud at the kitchen table, alone, because yesterday she had read it aloud to the class and watched Marcus fall asleep with his eyes open. Not closed. Open. That took a kind of commitment.

She counted something on the draft. Every sentence she'd written was long. She'd written them long on purpose, because long sentences seemed like more sentence for the money. Her first one had fourteen words, the next one had fifteen, the one after that had thirteen. They marched. They marched like a line of identical bricks, and apparently a line of identical bricks could put Marcus to sleep in under a minute.

The dilemma was this: cut them down, or mix them up. She tried cutting the weak adjectives first, the ones her teacher had circled in red, the verys and reallys and nicelies. That helped a little. The sentences got cleaner but they still marched, thirteen, twelve, thirteen, like a metronome nobody had asked for.

So she tried the other thing. She broke one long sentence in half and left the piece of it standing there on its own. "Nobody answered." Three words. Then a long sentence after it, then another short one. She read the new version out loud in the empty kitchen, slowly, the way she'd read to the class, and she could hear something change. Her voice had somewhere to go now. It sped up, slowed down, sped up again, like she was driving a bike over hills instead of a parking lot.

"It has rhythm," she said to the refrigerator. The refrigerator did not disagree.

She read it one more time to calibrate, timing herself with the microwave clock, and the whole thing felt about a minute shorter and a hundred percent less like a lullaby. It seemed logical, anyway, that Marcus's open-eyed sleep had been caused by the march of same-length sentences, and that a person needed a few short ones to break up the long ones, like rest stops. She underlined the short sentences in blue so she could see the pattern down the page: long, long, short, long, short, long. A heartbeat, sort of. Not a march.

At school the next day she raised her hand before her nerve could change its mind. She read the first paragraph, got to "Nobody answered," and looked up. Marcus was sitting straighter. He was actually blinking.

"You're not asleep," Kayla said.

"I'm deciding whether to be," said Marcus. "Keep going."

story:
Samantha taped the folded program to her bedroom mirror so she would see it while she practiced. The order of songs ran down the page, and at the bottom, in her music teacher's handwriting, was the note she kept rereading: "After the last song, exit stage left, row by row." She hummed the second verse of "Oh, Shenandoah," stopped, and looked at the note again.

The problem was the word "left." In the mirror behind her, her bedroom door appeared on the right, but Samantha knew it was really on the left, because a mirror flips things. The audience, she thought, would be like a mirror. They would face her. So when they looked at her, her left side would be on their right. If stage left meant the left side as the audience saw it, she would walk toward the piano. If it meant her own left, she would walk toward the drums. Two options, and no way to check the answer from her bedroom.

She needed a test. At school the next day, she found Marcus, who had been in last year's concert. "When Mr. Okafor said exit stage left, which way did you actually go?" Marcus pointed toward the gym's far side, the side away from the piano. Samantha stood where a singer would stand, faced the empty bleachers, and checked which hand was on that side. Her left. She worked it out on the spot: stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.

The night of the concert, the gym lights radiated heat down onto the rows of singers, and Samantha felt the last song approaching, imminent and unstoppable. When the final note ended, Mr. Okafor raised his hand toward the far wing. Row by row, the singers filed off. Priya, beside Samantha, started to turn toward the piano. Samantha caught her sleeve. "Stage left is our left," she whispered, "not the audience's." Priya turned, and they stepped off together into the dark wing, where Marcus was waiting with two bottles of water.

story:
Asher sat in the back row of his new classroom while the teacher talked about the election posters on the wall. "Some of these are propaganda," she said, "posters made to persuade you, not to inform you." Asher copied the word into his notebook, though his mind kept drifting to the moving truck parked outside his old house three states away. His whole life was in those boxes, and tomorrow he would have to face them.

He remembered the last night in the old house, when his sister Priya had dug through a mountain of boxes hunting for her bedsheets. "Nobody labeled anything," she had groaned, pulling out a frying pan, a lamp, and a box of comic books. Asher had stood in the doorway watching her work by flashlight, and an idea had started to digest slowly in his head. The boxes had no writing on them, just brown opaque flaps, all looking the same, so every single one had to be opened and searched. There had to be a better way.

Now, after his first day at the new school, he walked through the empty rooms of the new house. His parents wouldn't arrive with the truck until morning, but the first boxes, the ones they had shipped ahead, were stacked in the garage. Asher found a marker in his backpack and got to work. On each box he wrote two things: the room it belonged in, and what was inside. "Kitchen, pots and pans." "Priya's room, bedsheets." When the truck came, his uncle would only have to read a box once and carry it straight to the right place, instead of dropping everything in the living room like last time.

The next morning, the truck rumbled into the driveway. Asher handed boxes off the lift one by one, pointing with the marker. "Bathroom, up the stairs." "My room, second door." Priya grabbed a box, read the label, and grinned. "Bedsheets," she said. "You're a genius." By lunch, most of the boxes had already found their rooms, and Asher carried the last one, marked "My room, comic books," up the stairs two at a time.

Batting average said Marcus was right, and Benjamin did not enjoy that.

He started copying numbers into the spreadsheet, row after row, while eating chips over the keyboard. His mother paused at the doorway and remarked that the hygiene of a desk used as a cafeteria was not something she wanted to quantify, then left him to it. He was still sulking over the averages when he remembered Saturday at his uncle Ray's sports bar, the TV turned to a baseball classic, his uncle swirling his drink.

Benjamin sat up so fast the chair squeaked. On-base percentage. Not hits. Times a player reached base, walks included. He found the columns for walks, typed the formula, and dragged it down the whole sheet, watching new numbers appear like something rising to the surface of a lake.

When he re-sorted the players by the new column, Sam Okafor climbed from eleventh to third, and TJ Ruiz sank like a stone with a family. Sam walked constantly; it didn't look exciting, so nobody talked about it, but there he was on base, inning after inning, being quietly useful. Marcus was ranking players with half the picture. Benjamin spent another hour checking, re-checking, and making the chart prettier than it needed to be, because charts that looked official won arguments.

He pasted the chart into the group chat and waited, hands folded behind his head. Three dots appeared. Then Marcus replied: "ok but I was still right about the nachos." Benjamin typed back, "Send me the nacho data and we'll see," and hit send before he could reconsider his life choices.

story:
Hazel had forty dollars and a plan: new basketball shoes, the ones with the springy sole, if they went on sale before Saturday's tryouts. The mall food court smelled like pretzels, and above it all a video wall played the shoe ad on loop. "Everybody's switching," a deep voice said, while a hundred blurry feet stamped past the camera. A famous point guard Hazel kind of admired looked straight at her and said, "I don't lace up anything else." Then the screen flashed the words REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE in gold.

She stopped walking. Something about that ad was like the wartime posters she'd been digging through for her library project. She'd started with posters from the 1940s, stern faces and pointing fingers, and then found something better. In a dusty reference book she read that the Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. She'd written the sentence on an index card, but she hadn't really believed people needed lessons in spotting tricks. Now, standing under a thirty-foot shoe ad, she thought maybe they did.

She tested it like a game. First ad: "Everyone's switching." Her social studies teacher would say that was a bandwagon appeal, the same move as a poster showing a whole town buying war bonds. Second: REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE, words so vague they meant nothing, just loaded words, the book's term for language built to push feelings instead of facts. Third: the point guard. Would he really wear those shoes if the company didn't pay him? Celebrity testimonial, she scribbled on her hand with a pen from her pocket. Three tricks in one minute. She despised feeling handled, like her forty dollars had a target painted on it.

Inside the shoe store she picked up the box. The springy sole felt the same as the plain pair on the next shelf, which cost eighteen dollars less. An ambiguous sign said SALE, but the tiny print said "selected styles," and none of the selected styles were her size. "Can I try both?" she asked the clerk, a teenager named Priya who was balancing a stack of boxes one-handed while helping an older man find wide sizes.

Priya set the boxes down. "Smart question. Half the spring is the price tag, honestly." The older man chuckled. Hazel ran the length of the aisle in each pair. The cheaper ones gripped better on the slick floor; she could feel her cuts quicker. It wasn't proof, exactly, one run down one aisle, but it was evidence.

She bought the cheaper shoes, and with the leftover money she bought a pretzel and slid half of it across the table to a boy from her school, a refugee named Amir who'd arrived in the fall and usually sat alone with nothing from the food court. "For tryouts?" he asked, pointing at the box. "For tryouts," she said, and laced them up right there, double-knotted.

"Everybody's switching," she muttered at the video wall on her way out, and walked past it in her new shoes.

story:
Ellie had been on the couch for three days, and she was tired of soup. She propped herself up on the armrest and watched the vapor rise from her mug of lemon tea, curling and vanishing near the ceiling. Her throat still felt scratchy, and her nose was red from tissue after tissue. The math competition at school was on Friday, and she wanted more than anything to be back for it.

When Mom came home from the pharmacy, Ellie sat up with an abrupt bounce. "Did you get the medicine? The kind that kills germs?"

"Everything the doctor said to get," Mom said, holding up a bag of cough syrup, tissues, and popsicles.

"Not that. Antibiotics," Ellie said. "Lily's little brother had a sore throat, and he took antibiotics and got better fast. If I take them, I could be back at school by Friday."

Mom set down the bag. "That's for the doctor to decide. We have a video call with her in ten minutes."

When the call started, Ellie asked right away. "Can you prescribe antibiotics? I need to get better fast. I have a competition."

The doctor shook her head, not unkindly. "Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, so they wouldn't help you. A cold or the flu is a virus. Antibiotics just don't work on it."

Ellie frowned at the screen. "Then how do I get better?"

"Rest, fluids, time. Your body does the work."

So Ellie made a plan to conserve her energy. She spent Thursday on the couch doing practice problems in her head, drinking tea, and sleeping whenever her eyes got heavy. She noticed that the more she rested, the less her throat hurt, and by Friday morning her fever was gone and her nose had almost stopped running.

At school, she slid into her seat just as the competition papers were handed out. Lily leaned over. "You made it."

"Rest and fluids," Ellie whispered, "and a lot of nothing." She picked up her pencil and read the first problem.

By halftime Theo had made 4 of 10, and the scoreboard screen flashed his season average: 40 percent. In the third quarter he got hot, swishing five straight, and the average ticked up to 50. The announcer's voice boomed over the squeak of sneakers. "Theo Cardoso, up ten percentage points today, folks." Two rows down, a radio reporter said into her microphone, "That same jump is a 25 percent increase for the young guard."

Alexandre stopped chewing his popcorn. Ten and twenty-five, about the same shot? He wrote both numbers and stared at them, then leaned toward the reporter. "How can it be ten and also twenty-five?" She smiled but kept talking into her recorder, so he turned to his notebook instead. He counted the season totals again, slow and careful, the way he counted everything. Both phrases pointed the same direction, from 40 to 50. Maybe they were two doors into the same room. He wanted to disclose the trick to somebody before the buzzer.

Next to him, Marcus was scribbling a sign that said MARCUS SAW IT FIRST, because his older brother worked the scoreboard clock and Marcus wanted the whole gym to know. "Check this," Alexandre said, showing him the notebook. "Ten percentage points, or a 25 percent increase. Same change, different words." Marcus squinted, then grinned. "So when the paper says Theo improved 25 percent, he only made one more shot out of ten?"

"Exactly," Alexandre said. Coach Ramirez wrote something in a small book and underlined it twice, his face neutral as a locked door, though his prescription for winning was famous: defense first, always. Theo caught a pass at the top of the key, rose, and released.

The net snapped clean, and Marcus held his sign over his head.

The door banged open before Marcus could knock twice. It was Tasha, Dev's older sister, and she didn't say hi. "Take your shoes off and don't touch the kitchen," she snapped, then stomped upstairs. Marcus stood in the doorway holding his model rocket kit until Dev pulled him inside.

"She's like that," Dev said, spreading the kit across the living room carpet. "Always mad about something. Last week she yelled at me for breathing too loud." Marcus nodded, but something felt off. Tasha had helped him build a launch pad just last month, laughing the whole time. People didn't flip like a light switch for no reason, he thought, unless they were just that kind of person. He decided to test it. "Hey Dev, is anything going on with her?"

Dev shrugged. "How should I know? She's just rude."

They glued fins and taped the nose cone. Through the ceiling came footsteps, back and forth, back and forth, then a phone buzzing, then a long silence. Marcus kept one ear on it while his hands worked. He was beginning to build a second idea in his head: maybe Tasha's mood had a hidden cause, something he couldn't see, the way you can't see the wind but you can watch the flag.

At the tense moment, the footsteps stopped right above them, and a voice said, very quietly, "I'm sorry, Grandma. I'll come Saturday." Marcus froze with the glue tube in his hand. Dev looked up too.

Tasha came down a few minutes later, eyes red. "Sorry I barked at you guys. I just got a call. Grandma's in the hospital." She looked at the rocket spread across the floor. "That's a good one. Spontaneous combustion in the engine, right? That's what makes it go?" Marcus said yes, that was basically the motive power, fuel burning all at once. She almost smiled and went to make them popcorn.

Later, Dev's cousin Renard showed up and started complaining that a kid at school had slammed a door in his face that morning. "Total jerk," Renard said.

"Maybe," said Marcus. "Or maybe something happened to him you don't know about." He told them what he'd read in his brother's psychology book, holding it up to the light. "Psychologist Lee Ross named it the fundamental attribution error in 1977. We blame people's personality and skip their situation. Kind of like ants colonizing a whole picnic because one crumb fell, we spread the blame everywhere." Renard frowned, thinking. Then he picked up the spare nose cone and asked, "So when does this thing fly?"

Nolan got to Desh's house first, so he had the best view of the disaster. The science club's robot, built over three weekends for the county fair, sat dead in the middle of the garage, and the four members who arrived after him were already shouting.

"It's the battery," Marcus insisted. "I tested it Friday. It drains way too fast, like something is consuming all the power in ten minutes."

"You're wrong," Amelia said. "I watched the wheels on Saturday. The left one jerks. It's a motor problem."

Desh shook his head. "The wiring is the problem. I checked the circuits, and the backup sensor cable is pinched."

Nolan had been out of town and had seen nothing but a group chat full of arguing. Then Priya, the fifth member, was absent, sick with the flu. At her mother's suggestion, Nolan called her, and she asked him to read her text out loud to the group. He held up his phone.

"I only ever worked on the sensor that detects toxic gas," Nolan read. "I know that part works. I tested it with vinegar fumes Sunday. But I never saw the whole robot running. Someone else has to tell me about the rest."

Everyone went quiet. Nolan looked around the garage at four people who had each seen exactly one piece of the machine, and the shape of the argument suddenly made sense to him. He remembered a story his grandfather told him, from ancient India, about blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and then describe the animal completely differently. The one holding the trunk imagines a snake; the one at the leg insists it is a tree.

"It's the parable of the blind men and the elephant," he said. "That's us. We've each only touched one part."

Desh grinned slowly. "So nobody's wrong. Everybody's just holding a different piece." They ran the robot whole, with all systems on, and watched together. It lurched left because of the motor, and the motor strained because the pinched cable made the sensor draw too much power, which drained the battery and set off the toxic-gas alarm by the vinegar residue Priya had left inside.

"So Marcus's battery, Desh's cable, Amelia's wheel, and Priya's sensor were all real," Nolan said, unscrewing the pinched cable cover. "Just one at a time."

Twenty minutes later the robot rolled straight across the driveway, and Amelia whooped so loud that Desh's neighbor looked over the fence. Marcus filmed it on his phone to send to Priya, and at the end he added, "Your nose works. The whole elephant works."

story:
Mackenzie had read The Lighthouse of Hallow Bay three times, but for her book club report she needed something more than a summary. She carried the novel, a stack of yellow sticky notes, and a pencil to the reading nook by the window, where the afternoon light fell in a warm stripe across the cushion. She had decided on a small ritual: every time the blue door of the old boathouse appeared in the story, she would mark the page and write one sentence about what was happening there.

The first blue door showed up in chapter two, when the main character, Ivy, pressed her ear against it and dreamed of the father who had disappeared at sea. Mackenzie wrote "hope of his return" on the note and pressed it onto the page. In chapter five, Ivy hid behind the same door while her cousin searched for her, and in chapter nine, the door stood open, letting in the wind while the family argued inside. Mackenzie sat back and looked at her row of notes like a string of flags.

At the kitchen table that evening, her older brother Dev leaned over her shoulder. "What's with all the yellow paper?"

"Every time the blue door shows up, I mark it," Mackenzie said. "I'm trying to see if it means something different each time."

Dev nodded. "Recurring image like that is called a motif," he said, and went back to his sandwich.

In the nook the next morning, Mackenzie formulated a test. If the door really changed meaning, then the last time it appeared should be almost the opposite of the first. She found the final mention in chapter twenty: Ivy painting the door gray herself, the day she finally stopped waiting for news of her father. Mackenzie read the page twice, then peeled off her first sticky note and laid it beside the last one. Hope of his return, one said. Letting him go, said the other. Same door, same hinges, same blue paint, but by the end it meant something entirely different. She checked the middle notes and saw the pattern in order, hiding place, shelter, then farewell.

That afternoon Dev found her taping the sticky notes in a long line down the hallway, chapter by chapter, like train cars.

"You know that's going to leave marks on the wall," he said.

Mackenzie stood at the far end and looked down the row. "Look at it from here," she said. "It goes from blue to gray."

Eleanor set her fork down beside her meatloaf and stared at the newspaper folded next to her plate, because the draft for her current events report was due by email at eight o'clock tonight, and it was already six forty-five. The article she had chosen ranked quarterbacks by something called passer rating, and the numbers made no sense to her at all. One quarterback had 104.2. Another had 158.3, and the caption under his photo called it perfect.

"Why would a perfect score be a weird number like that?" she asked her brother Marcus, who was stacking green beans on his knife like he was building a wall.

Marcus shrugged. "It's just what it is. Football stuff." He wanted to finish dinner fast so he could colonize the whole living room couch before their cousin arrived, spreading his blanket and controller across every cushion like territory he claimed by sitting on it first.

"A hundred would be perfect," Eleanor insisted. "Like on a test. If the scale starts at zero and ends somewhere, perfect should end at one hundred." She flipped the paper over and ran her finger down the ranking column again, counting the quarterbacks listed there. Twelve names, twelve different numbers, all squeezed down from games she had never watched. Somewhere behind each number were completions and yards and touchdowns and interceptions, and all of it had been crushed together into a single figure, the way her school averaged test scores into one grade. But the top number still bothered her, hanging there like a picture she couldn't get to hang perpendicular to the floor.

"Maybe it's not out of a hundred," Marcus said through a mouthful of beans. "Maybe the whole scale is different."

Eleanor grabbed her mother's phone from the counter and typed "passer rating maximum" into the search box. She read, scrolled, and read again. "It says the passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number," she announced, "on a scale from zero to a maximum of 158.3." She set the phone down. "So a perfect rating isn't a hundred. It's a strange number, and it's the top of the whole scale."

Marcus had stopped stacking beans. "So that guy with 158.3 is literally the best you can be?"

"By the rating, yeah." Eleanor was already rewriting the first line of her report in her head. She had planned to argue that the rankings were unfair because her favorite team's quarterback sat seventh, but now she understood that his number was built from everything he had done all season, folded together. Seventh wasn't a judgment of him as a person. It was arithmetic. She picked her fork back up and speared a green bean off Marcus's abandoned wall.

At 7:58 she hit send, then carried her plate to the sink. Marcus had claimed the couch, blanket and all, and was waving the remote at her.

"Want to watch the highlights?" he asked. "That perfect guy plays tonight."

Eleanor dried her hands on the towel. "Show me the numbers at the end," she said, and sat down on the last free cushion.

Samuel's cleats were still damp from the morning dew when Coach Marisol dragged a thick rope out of the equipment shed and dropped it across the center circle. "Tug-of-war," she announced. "Championship Saturday has one at halftime, and we are going to win it."

Devon, who lived upstairs from Samuel in the apartment building where their families were tenants, threw both fists in the air. "I've been waiting all season for this!"

They pulled in pairs first, then four against four, then all eight. Samuel gripped the rope in the eight-on-eight round and noticed something strange. When it had been just him against Devon, his arms burned and his legs shook. Now, with the whole team heaving together, his pull felt easier. Lazy, almost. He glanced down the line. Marco was definitely leaning back less than before. When Coach blew her whistle and called the pull "sloppy," Marco's face went pink.

That night Samuel couldn't let it go. He pulled a strand of spaghetti from his dinner and tugged it, thinking. He could infer something from what he'd seen: the more people on the rope, the smaller each person's pull seemed to get. But was that real, or was he imagining it? The only way to find out was a test.

At Tuesday practice he begged Coach Marisol for the spring scale she used for fitness testing. She hooked it to the rope and the fence post. Devon pulled alone and the scale read ninety pounds. Then four boys pulled together, and Samuel did the math in his notebook. Devon's share of the four-man pull was smaller than his solo pull. Same for Marco. Same for everyone. The pattern held.

"You sound like my grandfather," Coach said, laughing. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

"Ringelmann," Samuel repeated, writing it down. "So what do we do about it?"

Coach rubbed her chin. "That, scientist, is your problem."

On Saturday, the stadium smelled like popcorn and cut grass, and the stands were louder than any game all season. At halftime, Samuel gathered his team in the end zone. "Every pull is your pull," he told them. "Nobody's hiding on this rope." He pointed at the opposing team's biggest puller, a tower of a kid. "He's not the rope. He's just one guy."

The whistle blew. Samuel planted his feet, kept his arms straight, and pulled as hard as if he were alone in his backyard. Down the line he heard Devon growling like a guard dog, and the rope came, inch by glorious inch, until the red flag crossed the chalk line. Devon tackled Samuel into the grass, and the whole team piled on, shouting, "Ringelmann!" at the sky.

story:
Maya's dog, Biscuit, flattened himself under the coffee table the second the thunder cracked, and Peyton watched him shake. "He's scared," Maya said, not looking up from her phone. "It's happening right now, the storm. He's freaked out by the actual thunder."

Peyton nodded slowly. Maya had been quiet all afternoon, checking the weather app, then the soccer app, then the weather again. Her cleats sat by the door, already double-knotted, though the tryout was still four days away. "You keep doing that," Peyton said, pointing at the phone. "Is there thunder in there?"

"No. It's the tryout list. They posted the roster numbers and mine is eleven, which is fine, but what if they move me to defense, what if I trip in the first drill, what if Coach Reyes already decided." Maya set the phone face down, then picked it up again. Peyton thought about Biscuit under the table. He was shaking at the thunder that was actually booming outside. Maya was shaking at thunder that had not happened yet and might never happen at all. "So Biscuit is scared of the storm," Peyton said, testing the idea out loud, "and you're not scared, exactly, because nothing's happening right now. It's more like you're worried about what might happen Friday. My mom says that's anxiety. Fear is the reaction to a threat happening now, and anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future."

Maya stopped scrolling. "So Biscuit has fear and I have anxiety."

"Basically."

"Great. The dog is more competent than me."

"He's hiding under a table," Peyton said. "You're sitting on a couch eating all my chips."

"That's my coping mechanism. Chips consume my stress." Maya held up the nearly empty bag as proof, and Peyton laughed and grabbed the last chip, calling a truce over the crumbs.

If somebody had named the game, he thought, they must have named it after the first thing they used as a goal. Not a hoop. Something that actually held the ball.

"Hey, Coach," he called across the room, "who made up basketball in the first place?"

She smiled a coach smile, the kind that gives away nothing. "Halftime, Carter. Three minutes."

Somebody found the emergency lamp and the little generator in the garage, and Mr. Alvarez yanked the cord until it coughed to life. The TV stayed dead, but the lamp lit the room, and Coach Henderson clapped her hands. "Halftime is halftime. Here's the question. Basketball was invented by a man named James Naismith. "Peach baskets!" Carter shouted before he could stop himself. "That's why it's called a basket!" The words were out, and now he had to back them up, fast, before Dev could contradict him with something confident and wrong. The room went quiet except for the generator humming in the garage. Coach Henderson slowly lifted the chocolate basketball off the mantel and weighed it in her hands.

"Nobody," she said, "has ever gotten all of that."

She tossed it underhand toward the beanbag, and Carter caught it against his chest with both arms.

She tested a small piece of scrap card first. She took a blunt spoon from the kitchen drawer and drew it firmly along a ruler's edge, pressing a shallow line into the card. Then she folded along that line, and the card bent straight and clean, with no crack at all. She blinked at it, then tried a second scrap without the pressed line, and it split like the others. It was not luck. She had been negligent about one small step, and the small step was everything.

The next card transformed under her hands. She scored a line with the spoon before folding, and the spine of the card came out smooth and sharp. On the front she drew tulips, then a border of little stars. Biscuit woke up, yawned, and put one paw on the envelope, as if signing it too.

"You can deliver it with me," Emilia said. She slid the card inside, and the white paper whispered against the edges. On the envelope she wrote her grandmother's name and, underneath, in small letters, "Folded with a spoon."

The group chat was called "Mud Dogs Rule," and it had been quiet all week until Tuesday night, when Marisol posted a screenshot of two baseball players with a single question: "Who's better?"

A minute later Marisol sent a laughing emoji and then a link. "Look at the combined number for both years together." Harper picked the tablet back up. She found the row, read it, and read it again. Marisol replied that her brother called it Simpson's paradox, and that it had a name because it happened in more places than baseball. Harper decided to test it herself. She pulled up her own basketball free throws from the rec league app, where she kept every practice logged. She sorted the sessions into two groups, took the percentages for each group, then the percentage for all of them together, and worked the numbers with a pencil on the back of her homework. Her percentages moved the same way when she combined groups, which meant the thing on the baseball site wasn't a typo. It was something numbers could just do.

She scrolled up through the chat and noticed something else. Dex, who never missed a chance to argue, hadn't posted at all. She sent him a private message: "You're quiet. You already knew about this, didn't you?"

His reply came as a long text. "OK yes. I found it last summer and I was going to use it to win an argument with you about whether our Mud Dogs season was really as bad as the league standings said. Our average runs per game over the whole season look fine, but that's because of two blowout games. I didn't want to say that out loud because everyone would say I was making excuses." She typed back, "Bring better granola tomorrow and I'll tell the chat the paradox myself." Then she pasted the link into the group chat with the message: "Justice had the higher average in 1995 and in 1996. Jeter had the higher average for the two years combined. Numbers can do that."

Dex answered in four seconds: "Treaty accepted. The granola will be fresh."

Brielle stood in the wings of the music classroom, clutching her flute, and watched Marcus pace. He was two performers ahead of her, and his hands were shaking so hard that his sheet music rattled like a window in a storm.

"You okay?" she whispered.

"My voice is going to crack," Marcus said. He swallowed hard. "My mouth is so dry, and my heart is going like a million miles an hour." He held out one hand so she could see the tremble for herself.

Brielle had felt exactly the same thing at last month's audition, and it had nearly wrecked her. That afternoon she had gone home and scrutinized the notes she'd copied from a science magazine in the library, reading every line twice. The article said stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline, it explained, can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice, and trembling hands. So her body wasn't breaking. It was doing what any organism does when it senses danger, even danger as harmless as forty kids with folding chairs. The weird part, the part she'd wondered about for days, was that her body couldn't actually tell the difference between a bear and a concert.

So she had tested an idea. At the audition, right before her turn, she had taken slow breaths and told herself, out loud in a tiny whisper, "Nothing here is attacking me. This is just a room." Her heart had still pounded, but her hands had gone steady enough to play.

She turned to Marcus now. "Try this," she said, and handed him her water bottle. "Sip. Then breathe with me, slow. And tell your body it's fight-or-flight stuff, that's all it is."

Marcus looked hesitant, but he sipped, and then they breathed together behind the curtain, in through the nose, out through the mouth, four slow times. Ms. Reyes called his name. He walked out, and Brielle watched his shoulders drop as he set his music on the stand.

His first note came out wobbly. His second one didn't. By the chorus he was singing full and clear, and when he finished, he grinned straight at the wings.

Then Ms. Reyes said, "Brielle, you're up."

Brielle walked to the front, lifted her flute, and whispered, "Just a room."

Sawyer refreshed the marketplace page for the third time that morning, and the Frost Dragon egg was still priced at four thousand gold. Last month it had been two thousand. He slumped in his chair, staring at the listing while his snow fox, Pip, curled up in the corner of the screen and began to hibernate, the way the game's pets always did when their owner ignored them too long.

Four thousand gold was impossible. He had been saving for weeks, selling bread from his bakery stall, because bread was a carbohydrate that every player's energy bar needed and it always sold. But at this rate, the dragon egg would stay out of reach forever. He scrolled through the listings and counted them. Only three eggs for sale in the whole market. Three weeks ago, when the price was two thousand, there had been nine.

He sat back. Fewer eggs, higher price. More bread, lower price, because bread was everywhere. Something invisible was pushing the numbers, like a hidden hand. He wanted to see if he was right, so he opened a notebook and started a chart: item, number of listings, price. Then his dad called from the hallway that they were driving to the hardware store.

At the gas station, while Dad filled the tank, a kid about Sawyer's age pointed at the sign. "Why did it go up since last week? It was cheaper." The station attendant, wiping his hands on a rag, shrugged. "Crude oil. The cost of crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so when crude oil goes up, the pump price goes up too." The kid's dad nodded like this was ordinary news, and Sawyer stood there with his hand on the door of the car, thinking. A price could move because of something far away that you never saw. Crude oil for gasoline. Scarcity for dragon eggs. Maybe the same rule, wearing different clothes.

Back home, he tested his idea. He spent his gold on a cheap fertile soil seed instead of the egg, planted it in his garden plot, and waited three days while more players hatched dragon events. By Saturday, the marketplace showed eleven Frost Dragon eggs, and the price had slid to one thousand eight hundred. Sawyer bought one. In his notebook, under the chart, he wrote "scarce = up, plentiful = down" and drew an arrow. Then he set the egg beside the sleeping Pip, tapped it once, and whispered, "Okay, buddy, wake up. You're about to have company."

Grandma had been at the house since Monday, and by Wednesday Laurence had given up saying whole sentences to her at the park. She would shout across the picnic table by the duck pond, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned to look, and Grandma would still tilt her head and say, "What's that, dear? Speak up." Laurence couldn't understand it, because Grandma heard the ice cream truck's jingle from three blocks away, and she caught every word the deep-voiced park ranger said when he warned everyone about the geese. It was only Laurence's own voice that vanished.

Sitting on the bench, Laurence turned the puzzle over. Grandma had said her hearing was "mostly there, just blurry." Blurry sound. She thought about how the pond's shallow edge bent the light so the stones looked displaced, the way a straw in a glass seemed to refract into two pieces. Maybe sound could get blurry too, and maybe not all sound the same way. The ranger's low voice had come through fine. The ice cream truck, the wind in the reeds, the men playing chess, all low, all clear. Her own voice, and the shrieking little kids near the swings, all high, all lost. She felt a flicker of skepticism about her own idea, because it seemed too simple, but simple was worth testing.

She slid closer to Grandma and dropped her voice into the low register she used for reading the villain's part in class plays. "Grandma. The ducks stole my sandwich." She kept it quiet, quieter than a normal sentence, almost a mumble.

Grandma laughed out loud. "Both of them? Those fundamental criminals of the pond, always after the bread."

"You heard me?" Laurence said, still low. "I barely said it out loud."

"Loud enough, dear. It just wasn't all fuzzy." Grandma shook her head. "The doctor told me years ago, high-pitched sounds go first. I thought he meant bells and whistles. I didn't know my own granddaughter would count."

For the rest of the week, Laurence practiced her low voice until it felt like a coat she could put on. On Friday at the park, she leaned toward Grandma and rumbled, "The ice cream man is coming. My treat."

Grandma was already holding out her hand for coins.

Jace had planted his tomato, pepper and squash seedlings on the first warm Saturday of April, certain that warm meant safe. "You're my tenants now," he told the little green rows, patting the soil around them, "and I'm the landlord who waters you." For two weeks they grew, and he thought the hard part was over.

Then the radio said thirty-four degrees tomorrow night, and Jace stood in the backyard frowning at the sky. Warm days had fooled him. He tried to remember what his grandfather had said last summer while picking peppers: "Can't put these out till after the last spring frost. Freezing kills them." Frost. That was the hidden thing, the cold that came at night when nobody was watching.

He wasn't sure the cold would really reach his plants, so he tested it. He covered every bed with old sheets and buckets, except one squash seedling that he left open on purpose, the far corner of the yard away from the house wall. If that one drooped by morning, he would know for certain it was the cold and not something else, like the neighbor's cat or too much water.

Morning came gray and glittering. Under the sheets the tomatoes stood stiff and fine, leaves untouched. The uncovered squash lay flat, its edges blackened and thin as wet paper. Jace knelt beside it, sorry he had needed proof at all. "That wasn't trivial," he said quietly. "That was your whole life." He decided to revise his plan completely: no more planting until frost season was truly over, and he would keep a journal by the window to track each cold snap.

He buried the squash by the fence, then heard the back gate. His little sister Mira stood holding her blanket. "Is it safe now?" she asked. Jace draped his biggest sheet over the pepper bed one more time and nodded. "Safe," he said. "Come on, let's count buds."

Lydia sat in the emergency room with her left wrist propped on a pillow, remembering the last time she had sat in this exact chair, two summers ago, holding the exact same wrist. Her older brother Theo had leaned in, squinting. "Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off." He had read it somewhere, and Lydia had tested it right there in the exam room, squeezing a tennis ball with each hand. The right hand bounced the ball hard off the wall. Now, waiting for the X-ray results, Lydia ran her thumb along her right forearm, which was currently her good arm but would soon be her only arm. "Hey, Theo," she said. The doctor came back with the X-ray and said what Lydia already guessed: broken, cast, six weeks. Theo helped her write LEFT ARM: WANTED FOR HARD LABOR on the plaster before the ink could smear.

"So," Lydia said, wiggling the fingers that stuck out of the cast, "who's bringing me the tennis ball?"

Maya woke to a strange brightness and found the window filled with white. School was closed, the radio said, and her little brother Theo came bouncing into her room in his dinosaur pajamas before she could even find her socks.

The backyard had turned into a flat white plateau, level and smooth, except where the picnic table poked through like a buried boat. She held her mitten out flat and let the snowfall settle on it. The first flakes melted almost instantly, but when she turned her hand toward the shaded side of the porch, where the air was colder, they held their shape. She bent close. Six arms. "Water links up six-sided when it freezes," she said. "So the flakes come out with six sides. Six arms. Every single time." She looked up at the millions of flakes still falling, each one of them six-sided, and felt like she had a secret about the whole sky.

Later they built the snowman on the white plateau of the yard, and Theo insisted on giving it a red scarf because, he said, red was Dad's favorite color and would symbolize him being home early on snow days. When they went inside, their mugs of cocoa were waiting, and Mom warned them not to sniff the bottle of glass cleaner she was using on the window, because it was toxic. Maya drank her cocoa slowly. Before the flakes on her mitten vanished, she had scooped one last big lacy one onto a black notebook cover and carried it to the freezer, where it waited, six perfect arms intact, on the shelf next to the peas. "I'll show Ms. Alvarez on Monday," she said, and closed the freezer door.

story:
Muhammad stood in the living room holding a candle like it was a prestigious trophy, even though it was just dripping wax on a saucer. The power had cut out an hour ago, and his big sister Zainab was stretched on the couch reading by her phone light. Muhammad's stomach growled so loudly that they both heard it.

"Snack time," he announced, and marched to the refrigerator. He opened the door, stared into the dark cold shelves, saw nothing he wanted, and shut it. Two minutes later he opened it again. And again. On the fourth try, Zainab appeared beside him holding her candle.

"Muhammad, stop. The fridge only keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, if the door stays closed. Every time you open it, you're spending that time." Muhammad blinked at her, then at the fridge, doing the math in his head. He had opened it five times. "So we decide first, then open it once?" he said slowly. "Exactly once," Zainab said. "Like a game show. One pick, no changing your answer."

Muhammad felt his conscience poke him about all those openings, so he made it right. He sat by the candle and wrote a note by hand, which felt hilariously old-fashioned: "Dear Fridge, I have chosen the leftover biryani and one mango juice. I will not peek. Signed, Muhammad." Zainab read it over his shoulder and laughed so hard she nearly snorted out the candle flame. They folded the letter, tucked it under the fridge magnet for proof, and retired to the couch to wait out the dark like brave explorers.

When the clock showed the hour they'd agreed on, Muhammad leapt up, announced "One pick!", flung the door open, grabbed the biryani container and juice in a single sweep, and shut the door with a triumphant bang. "Nailed it," he said, raising the juice like a trophy. Zainab handed him a fork. "Game show champion," she said. "Now eat before the candle retires."
